items.q: **Schedule(Theatre, MovieTitle, Time)** — Time is stored in 24-hr format (6 pm = 18:00). Write a relational-algebra expression to list the **theatre name and time** where we can watch the movie **"FindingNemo" after 3 pm**.
items.answer: $$\Pi_{Theatre,\,Time}\big(\sigma_{MovieTitle='FindingNemo'\;\wedge\;Time\ge 15{:}00}(Schedule)\big)$$ **Select** the rows for FindingNemo at 15:00 or later (σ), then **project** the theatre and time columns (∏).

items.q: Give the relational-algebra expression equivalent to the query tree: project **Pnumber, Dnum, Lname, Address, Bdate** from PROJECTs located in **'Surat'**, joined to their DEPARTMENT and that department's manager EMPLOYEE.
items.answer: $$\Pi_{Pnumber,\,Dnum,\,Lname,\,Address,\,Bdate}\Big(\big(\sigma_{Plocation='Surat'}(Project)\bowtie_{Dnum=Dnumber} Department\big)\bowtie_{Mgr\_ssn=Ssn} Employee\Big)$$ Filter projects in Surat → **theta-join** to Department on `Dnum=Dnumber` → theta-join to Employee on `Mgr_ssn=Ssn` → project the required columns. (Read a query tree **bottom-up**: leaves are base relations, internal nodes are operations.)

items.q: **EMPLOYEE(Emp-ID, Salary, Deduction, Years-of-Service)** — compute a report **Report(Emp-ID, Net_Salary, Bonus, Tax)** where Net_Salary = Salary − Deduction, Bonus = 2000 × Years-of-Service, Tax = Salary × 25%.
items.answer: Use **generalized projection** (arithmetic allowed in the project list): $$Report \leftarrow \Pi_{Emp\text{-}ID,\;(Salary-Deduction),\;(2000\times YearsOfService),\;(Salary\times 0.25)}(EMPLOYEE)$$ Generalized projection extends ∏ to allow **arithmetic expressions** over attributes, renamed to Net_Salary, Bonus and Tax.

items.q: **SALESPERSON(SalesPersonID, Name)**, **TRIP(SalesPersonID, From, To, TripID)**, **EXPENSE(TripID, Amount)**. (a) Print the ID & name of salesmen who took trips to **Delhi**. (b) Print the **total trip expenses** of the salesperson whose ID is **504**.
items.answer: **(a)** $t1 \leftarrow \sigma_{To='Delhi'}(TRIP)$; $t2 \leftarrow \Pi_{SalesPersonID}(t1)$; $Result \leftarrow \Pi_{SalesPersonID,Name}(SALESPERSON \bowtie t2)$ — select Delhi trips, get the salesperson IDs, join to SALESPERSON for names. **(b)** $t1 \leftarrow \sigma_{SalesPersonID=504}(TRIP)$; $t2 \leftarrow \Pi_{TripID}(t1)$; $t3 \leftarrow EXPENSE \bowtie t2$; $Result \leftarrow \mathcal{F}_{SUM(Amount)}(t3)$ — find 504's trips, join their expenses, and **aggregate with SUM**.

items.q: For the schema in the previous question, give the **trip details (incl. amount)** for the trip whose expense **exceeded ₹10,000**.
items.answer: $t1 \leftarrow \sigma_{Amount>10000}(EXPENSE)$; $$Result \leftarrow \Pi_{SalesPersonID,From,To,TripID,Amount}\big(TRIP \bowtie_{TRIP.TripID=t1.TripID} t1\big)$$ Select the expensive expense rows, then join back to TRIP on `TripID` to recover the full trip details, and project them with the amount.

items.q: **Schedule(Theatre, Title, Time)**, **Movies(Title, Director, Actor)**, **Produced(Producer, Title)**, **Watch(Spectator, Title)**, **Liked(Spectator, Title)**. List the **producers who produced a movie that does NOT appear in a theatre**. Also: in which join are the non-matching tuples of both relations ignored?
items.answer: **"Does not appear" ⇒ set difference.** Titles not scheduled: $NotShown \leftarrow \Pi_{Title}(Produced) - \Pi_{Title}(Schedule)$. Then $$Result \leftarrow \Pi_{Producer}\big(Produced \bowtie NotShown\big)$$ — producers of those unscheduled titles. **Join:** the non-matching tuples of *both* R and S are dropped in the **(inner) join** (an outer join would keep them).

items.q: **Clients(CID, name, phone)**, **Staff(SID, name)**, **Appointments(CID, SID, date, time, service)**. Find the **appointment time and client name** of all appointments for staff member **"Anusha" on Feb 14**.
items.answer: $$\Pi_{time,\;Clients.name}\Big(\sigma_{Staff.name='Anusha'\;\wedge\;date='Feb\,14'}\big(Appointments \bowtie Clients \bowtie_{Appointments.SID=Staff.SID} \rho_{Staff}\big)\Big)$$ Join Appointments to Clients (on CID) and Staff (on SID), filter to staff *Anusha* on *Feb 14*, then project the appointment time and the client's name. (Rename is used so the two `name` columns don't clash.)

items.q: For an Account schema with **Depositor(cust_name, acc_no)**, **Borrower(cust_name, loan_no)** and **Loan(loan_no, branch, amount)**: (a) names of customers with **an account OR a loan**; (b) customers with **an account but no loan**; (c) names of customers with loans at the **Seattle branch** (without using join).
items.answer: **(a) Union:** $\Pi_{cust\_name}(Depositor)\;\cup\;\Pi_{cust\_name}(Borrower)$. **(b) Set difference:** $\Pi_{cust\_name}(Depositor)\;-\;\Pi_{cust\_name}(Borrower)$ (account **minus** loan). **(c) Without join** — use a selection over the Cartesian product, or nest: $\Pi_{cust\_name}\big(\sigma_{Borrower.loan\_no=Loan.loan\_no\,\wedge\,branch='Seattle'}(Borrower \times Loan)\big)$. *Mnemonic: "or" → ∪, "without/not" → −, "every/all" → ÷.*

items.q: Explain the different **levels of data abstraction** in a database system with a neat diagram (5M). Also state **logical data independence** and **physical data independence** (3M).
items.answer:
**Three levels:** **Physical/internal** (how data is stored — files, indexes), **Logical/conceptual** (what data + relationships, hiding storage), **View/external** (the part a user sees). Lowest = physical, highest = view; the DBMS maps between them.

**Physical data independence** — change the storage/internal schema (add an index, change file organisation) **without** altering the logical schema. **Logical data independence** — change the logical schema (add an attribute) **without** changing external views/applications. Logical independence is **harder** to achieve.

items.q: Elucidate the **three-schema architecture** with a neat diagram. Explain the levels involved and its advantages.
items.answer:
The **ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture** separates user views from physical storage: **External** (multiple user views), **Conceptual** (the whole DB's logical structure — entities, relationships, constraints), **Internal** (physical storage). Two mappings connect them (external↔conceptual, conceptual↔internal).

**Advantages:** **data independence** (a change at one level doesn't propagate up), **multiple customised views** of the same data, and **security** (users see only their view).

items.q: What is a **database**? Why are databases important in modern applications? Differentiate a **database** from a **DBMS**.
items.answer: A **database** is a logically-coherent collection of *related* data about a mini-world. They matter because modern apps store, query and share **large, interrelated** data **concurrently, consistently and securely** — beyond flat files. **Database vs DBMS:** the database is the **data**; the **DBMS** is the **software** that **defines, constructs, manipulates and shares** it (queries, concurrency, recovery, security).

items.q: Define DBMS, and write the **purpose of using a DBMS over File Processing Systems** on four key purposes.
items.answer: A **DBMS** is general-purpose software to define, construct, manipulate and share databases. **Purposes over file systems:** ① **control redundancy** (no duplicated/inconsistent copies); ② **enforce integrity & atomicity** (constraints; all-or-none transactions); ③ **concurrent multi-user access** without anomalies; ④ **security, backup & recovery** plus **program-data independence** (structure in the catalog, not hard-coded). File systems suffer redundancy, isolation, integrity, atomicity, concurrency and security problems.

items.q: What information is represented by **participation constraint** and **cardinality ratio** in an ER diagram? Illustrate with examples.
items.answer:
**Cardinality ratio** = the **maximum** relationship instances an entity can take — **1:1, 1:N, M:N**. e.g. an EMPLOYEE manages ≤1 DEPARTMENT and a DEPARTMENT has one manager → 1:1; a DEPARTMENT has many EMPLOYEEs → 1:N.

**Participation constraint** = the **minimum** participation — **total** (every entity must participate; double line) or **partial**. e.g. every EMPLOYEE must work for a DEPARTMENT → total; not every EMPLOYEE manages → partial.

items.q: With respect to the ER model, define: (i) Strong entity (ii) Participation constraint (iii) Cardinality ratio (iv) Recursive relationship (v) Weak entity (vi) Composite attribute.
items.answer: **(i) Strong entity** — has its own **key**; exists independently. **(ii) Participation** — minimum: **total** (double line) or **partial**. **(iii) Cardinality ratio** — max instances: 1:1/1:N/M:N. **(iv) Recursive relationship** — a relationship of an entity type **with itself** (role names), e.g. EMPLOYEE *supervises* EMPLOYEE. **(v) Weak entity** — **no key of its own**; identified by an **owner** + a **partial key/discriminator** (double rectangle). **(vi) Composite attribute** — divisible into parts, e.g. `Name → {Fname, Minit, Lname}`.

items.q: Mention the **steps in converting an ER diagram to a Relational Schema**.
items.answer: **(1)** Strong entity → relation; key → PK. **(2)** Weak entity → relation with owner's PK as FK; PK = owner PK + discriminator. **(3)** Composite → store leaf parts; **multivalued** → separate relation + entity PK. **(4) 1:1** → one side's PK as FK in the other. **(5) 1:N** → the **1-side's PK** as a **FK on the N-side**. **(6) M:N** → a **junction relation** with both PKs (composite PK) + relationship attributes. **(7) n-ary** → relation with all participants' PKs.

items.q: **Person(name,age,gender)**, **Frequents(name,pizzeria)**, **Eats(name,pizza)**, **Serves(pizzeria,pizza,price)**. In Relational Algebra: (a) pizzerias frequented by someone under 18; (b) females who eat **mushroom OR pepperoni**; (c) females who eat **mushroom AND pepperoni**.
items.answer: **(a)** $\Pi_{pizzeria}\big(Frequents \bowtie \sigma_{age<18}(Person)\big)$. **(b)** $\Pi_{name}\big(\sigma_{gender='F'}(Person)\bowtie \sigma_{pizza='mushroom' \vee pizza='pepperoni'}(Eats)\big)$. **(c)** AND across different rows needs **intersection**: $\Pi_{name}(\sigma_{gender='F'}(Person)\bowtie\sigma_{pizza='mushroom'}(Eats)) \cap \Pi_{name}(\sigma_{gender='F'}(Person)\bowtie\sigma_{pizza='pepperoni'}(Eats))$.

items.q: Explain **equi join** and **natural join** in relational algebra with an example, and justify their usage.
items.answer: An **equi join** $R\bowtie_{R.A=S.B}S$ matches tuples where the join attributes are **equal**, keeping **both** columns. A **natural join** $R\bowtie S$ is an equi join on **all common-named attributes** that **drops the duplicate** column. e.g. `EMPLOYEE ⋈ DEPARTMENT` on `Dno=Dnumber`. They are used to **follow foreign-key links** and combine related rows from multiple tables without spurious tuples.

items.q: Discuss the **entity integrity** and **referential integrity** constraints. Why is each important?
items.answer: **Entity integrity** — the **primary key cannot be NULL** (and is unique); important because the PK uniquely identifies each tuple, so a null PK makes rows indistinguishable. **Referential integrity** — a **foreign key** must be **NULL or match an existing PK** in the referenced relation; important to keep relationships **consistent** (no FK pointing to a non-existent row).

items.q: Enlist **3 different types of attributes** with one example each and the ER notation used.
items.answer: **Composite** — divisible into parts, e.g. `Address → {street, city, pin}` (oval with sub-ovals). **Multivalued** — a set of values, e.g. `PhoneNumbers` (**double oval**). **Derived** — computed from others, e.g. `Age` from `Bdate` (**dashed oval**). (Also: simple = single oval; key = underlined.)
